> **Slides vs lab.** Slides expand Prophet theory (trend, Fourier season, holidays).
> This lab runs the Beer bake-off, then fits Prophet two ways: through `fable.prophet`
> (inside the `fable` workflow) and through Meta's standard `prophet` package.
> **Prophet is optional**: each Prophet chunk skips cleanly if its package is not installed.

# Packages

```{r}
library(fpp3)
```

# Recall: Prophet model

\[
y_t = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + \varepsilon_t
\]

- $g(t)$: piecewise-linear trend with changepoints  
- $s(t)$: Fourier seasonality (`season(period, order)`)  
- $h(t)$: holiday dummies (optional)  

For quarterly Beer, set `period = 4` explicitly (defaults assume daily-or-finer data).

# Beer bake-off: SNAIVE, ETS, ARIMA, DHR

Same hold-out as Sessions 5 / 12: train through **2007 Q4**.

```{r}
beer <- aus_production |> filter(!is.na(Beer))
train <- beer |> filter_index(. ~ "2007 Q4")
test <- beer |> filter_index("2008 Q1" ~ .)

fit <- train |>
  model(
    snaive = SNAIVE(Beer),
    ets = ETS(Beer),
    arima = ARIMA(Beer),
    dhr = ARIMA(Beer ~ fourier(K = 2) + PDQ(0, 0, 0))
  )
fc <- fit |> forecast(h = nrow(test))
accuracy(fc, beer) |> select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |> arrange(RMSE)
fc |> autoplot(beer, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Method bake-off on Beer (hold-out from 2008 Q1)")
```

# Optional: Prophet (guarded)

```{r}
if (requireNamespace("fable.prophet", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(fable.prophet)
  set.seed(2026)  # Prophet's fit is not deterministic: seed it so your numbers match the slides
  fit_prophet <- train |>
    model(
      prophet = prophet(Beer ~ season(period = 4, order = 2))
    )
  fc_prophet <- fit_prophet |> forecast(h = nrow(test))
  # print(): inside if {}, only the last value would be shown otherwise
  print(accuracy(fc_prophet, beer) |> select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE))
  # Components (trend / season) - useful for communication slides
  print(fit_prophet |> components() |> autoplot())
} else {
  message("fable.prophet not installed - skipping Prophet chunk")
  message("Install with install.packages('fable.prophet') if you have a Stan toolchain.")
}
```

## All five methods together

Put the Prophet forecast next to the bake-off: one accuracy table and one panel per model
(as on the slides). Same training data, same test quarters, so the comparison is fair.

```{r}
if (exists("fc_prophet")) {
  fc_all <- bind_rows(fc, fc_prophet)
  print(accuracy(fc_all, beer) |> select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |> arrange(RMSE))
  print(
    fc_all |>
      autoplot(beer |> filter_index("2005 Q1" ~ .), level = NULL) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date(yearquarter("2008 Q1")),
                 linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
      facet_wrap(~.model, nrow = 1) +
      scale_x_yearquarter(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
      labs(title = "Beer hold-out: each model's forecast (colour) vs actuals (black)",
           subtitle = "Dashed = start of test, 2008 Q1", y = "Megalitres", x = NULL) +
      theme(legend.position = "none")
  )
} else {
  message("No Prophet forecast - the comparison above has four methods only.")
}
```

Does Prophet beat SNAIVE? ETS? Where does its forecast miss: level, seasonal shape, or both?

# Optional: the standard `prophet` package

`fable.prophet` is a wrapper: underneath, it calls Meta's `prophet` package
(documentation: <https://meta.github.io/prophet/>). Most Prophet tutorials, and the Python
version, use this standard interface directly. It fits the **same model** but works differently:

| | `fable.prophet` | `prophet` |
|---|---|---|
| Data | `tsibble` | data frame with columns `ds` (date) and `y` |
| Seasonality | `season(period = 4)` in quarters | `add_seasonality(period = 365.25)` in **days** |
| Forecast | `forecast(fit, h = 10)` | `predict(m, make_future_dataframe(m, 10, freq = "quarter"))` |
| Evaluation | `accuracy()`, `stretch_tsibble()` | compute by hand; `cross_validation()` |

```{r prophet-check}
has_prophet <- requireNamespace("prophet", quietly = TRUE)
if (!has_prophet) {
  message("prophet not installed - skipping this section.")
  message("Install with install.packages('prophet') (needs a Stan toolchain).")
}
```

## Data: `ds` and `y`

`prophet` needs real dates. `as.Date()` turns each quarter into its first day.

```{r, eval = has_prophet}
library(prophet)
df_train <- train |> as_tibble() |> transmute(ds = as.Date(Quarter), y = Beer)
df_test <- test |> as_tibble() |> transmute(ds = as.Date(Quarter), y = Beer)
head(df_train)
```

## Fit

Prophet's automatic seasonalities assume daily data: yearly with order 10, plus weekly and
daily. With 4 observations a year, switch them off and add one yearly season with
`fourier.order = 2`, the same model as `season(period = 4, order = 2)` above. The period is
365.25 because `prophet` measures time in days.

```{r, eval = has_prophet}
set.seed(2026)  # the interval bands are simulated
m <- prophet(yearly.seasonality = FALSE, weekly.seasonality = FALSE,
             daily.seasonality = FALSE)
m <- add_seasonality(m, name = "yearly", period = 365.25, fourier.order = 2)
m <- fit.prophet(m, df_train)
```

`prophet()` with no data only builds the specification; `fit.prophet()` estimates it.

## Forecast

```{r, eval = has_prophet}
future <- make_future_dataframe(m, periods = nrow(df_test), freq = "quarter")
fcst <- predict(m, future)
tail(fcst[, c("ds", "yhat", "yhat_lower", "yhat_upper")])
```

`future` holds the training dates **plus** 10 new quarters, so `fcst` contains fitted values
and forecasts together. `yhat_lower` / `yhat_upper` form an **80%** interval by default
(`interval.width`).

```{r, eval = has_prophet}
plot(m, fcst) + add_changepoints_to_plot(m) +
  labs(title = "prophet: Beer forecast with detected changepoints",
       x = NULL, y = "Megalitres")
prophet_plot_components(m, fcst)
```

The red dashed lines are changepoints whose slope change is not shrunk to zero. All 25
candidates lie in the first 80% of the training data: the last 20% has none, so the final
slope is carried forward unchanged.

## Hold-out accuracy and interval coverage

There is no `accuracy()` here: join the forecasts to the test set and compute the measures.

```{r, eval = has_prophet}
res <- df_test |>
  left_join(fcst |> transmute(ds = as.Date(ds), yhat, yhat_lower, yhat_upper),
            by = "ds")
res |>
  summarise(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((y - yhat)^2)),
    MAE = mean(abs(y - yhat)),
    MAPE = 100 * mean(abs((y - yhat) / y)),
    coverage_80 = mean(y >= yhat_lower & y <= yhat_upper)
  )
```

RMSE should be close to the `fable.prophet` result: same model, same data. `coverage_80` is
the share of test quarters inside the 80% interval. Compare with ETS:

```{r, eval = has_prophet}
fc |>
  filter(.model == "ets") |>
  hilo(80) |>
  unpack_hilo(`80%`) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(test |> as_tibble() |> select(Quarter, actual = Beer), by = "Quarter") |>
  summarise(coverage_80 = mean(actual >= `80%_lower` & actual <= `80%_upper`))
```

With only 10 test quarters, each quarter moves coverage by 10 points: treat this as a hint,
not proof. FPP3's warning is that Prophet's intervals ignore leftover residual
autocorrelation and so tend to be **too narrow**.

## Rolling-origin evaluation

One hold-out is not a final verdict. `cross_validation()` refits the model at several cutoffs
**inside the training data** and forecasts 2 years ahead from each: the same idea as
`stretch_tsibble()`. The test set stays untouched.

```{r, eval = has_prophet}
cv <- cross_validation(m, initial = 30 * 365.25, period = 2 * 365.25,
                       horizon = 2 * 365.25, units = "days")
length(unique(cv$cutoff))  # number of forecast origins
performance_metrics(cv, rolling_window = 1) |>
  transmute(horizon_years = round(as.numeric(horizon, units = "days") / 365.25, 1),
            rmse, mae, mape = 100 * mape, coverage)
```

`rolling_window = 1` averages over all horizons up to 2 years. Use these numbers, not the
test set, to choose between Prophet settings.

# Your turn

1. Fill a small table: method, RMSE, interpretability (H/M/L), one residual note.
2. If Prophet ran: does it beat ETS/ARIMA on this hold-out? Relate to FPP3's warning.
3. When would you present Prophet components to a product manager? When would you insist on an ARIMA+regression bake-off for a risk audience?
4. Standard `prophet`: refit with `changepoint.prior.scale = 0.005` and `0.5` (default
   `0.05`). Choose a value using the `cross_validation()` RMSE only, then check the test set
   **once**. Why would picking the value with the lowest **test** RMSE be cheating?
5. Standard `prophet`: change `fourier.order` from 2 to 10, the automatic default for yearly
   seasonality. What happens to the components plot and the hold-out RMSE? Why can 4
   observations a year not identify 10 sine/cosine pairs?
